fatal_errors: The proposed W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf refractory alloy does not reconstruct the nominally equimolar Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti system or its target FCC/BCC phase constitution.
The cited 40-hour milling evidence concerns NbMoTaWVTi and reports TiO precipitation after SPS, so it does not establish a precipitate-free dual-BCC bulk W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy.

The falsification experiment verifies grain size, phases, and strength but does not distinguish Hall-Petch strengthening from simple solid-solution strengthening because it lacks specimens with independently varied grain size at fixed composition and phase fractions.

The claim that low VEC prevents brittle intermetallic formation is too strong; VEC mainly predicts broad FCC/BCC tendencies and is not sufficient to establish phase stability or suppress intermetallics.
explanation: The hypothesis aligns with the broad processing concept: mechanical alloying followed by SPS can generate high defect density, refine grains, and retain metastable solid solutions. It also identifies reasonable instability limits involving elevated-temperature grain growth and milling-induced contamination. However, it is a different alloy family, uses a substantially different milling duration, proposes two BCC solutions rather than the target 83% FCC/17% BCC structure, and omits the target SPS details and hardness/density outcomes. Its predicted yield strength and improved ductility derive from a different refractory-alloy precedent. Evidence discipline is weak because the strongest cited processing example explicitly forms TiO during SPS and attributes part of the strength to precipitation, contrary to the proposed precipitate-free mechanism. A discriminating test should compare otherwise identical specimens with different grain sizes while holding composition, phase fractions, porosity, and contamination constant, then test whether strength follows Hall-Petch scaling beyond the solid-solution baseline.
